blocks.text: A **heap** is a binary tree that always keeps its **smallest** value at the top — or, in a **max-heap**, its **largest**. Reading that top value takes **O(1)**. Adding a value or removing the top takes **O(log n)**, however many values the heap holds.

That makes a heap the standard way to build a **priority queue**: a line where the most important item is served next, not the one that arrived first. Hospitals triage that way, operating systems schedule that way, and so do maps apps finding the shortest route.

blocks.alt: Two heaps holding the numbers 1 to 7. Left, a min-heap with 1 at the top: every parent is smaller than its children. Right, a max-heap with 7 at the top: every parent is larger than its children.
blocks.caption: The top of a heap is always its smallest value (min-heap) or its largest (max-heap).

items: **Shape — a complete binary tree.** Every level is full except possibly the last, and the last level fills from the **left**, with no gaps.
**Order — the heap property.** In a **min-heap** every parent is **less than or equal to** its children. In a **max-heap** every parent is **greater than or equal to** them.

blocks.text: Walk up from any node and, in a min-heap, every step leads to a smaller or equal value. So the root is the smallest value in the whole tree — without the heap ever comparing it with the far-away nodes.

blocks.alt: Three trees. Left: a valid min-heap, 2 on top, then 5 and 3, then 9, 6 and 8. Middle: not a heap, because 3 has a right child 8 but no left child, so the last level has a gap. Right: not a heap, because 4 sits below 5, and a child may not be smaller than its parent.

blocks.text: Only the top is in order

A heap is **not sorted**. Along any path from the root down, values never decrease — but nothing is promised **across** branches. Siblings can be in either order, and a value on the bottom level can be smaller than one higher up on another branch.

blocks.alt: The min-heap 1, 3, 2, 7, 4, 6, 5. The path 1, 3, 7 from the root down only grows. But the root's children, 3 and 2, are not in order, and the bottom level reads 7, 4, 6, 5.

blocks.text: Keeping only this much order is exactly what makes a heap cheap. A sorted array also keeps its smallest value at one end, but inserting into it shifts up to n values. A heap only ever repairs **one path** — about log₂ n nodes.

Because the tree is complete, it has no gaps — so a heap is stored as a plain **array**, level by level, left to right. There are no node objects and no pointers: positions do the linking. For the node at index `i`:

blocks.alt: The min-heap 1, 3, 2, 7, 4, 6, 5 drawn as a tree with each node's array index under it, and as the array underneath. The node at index 1, value 3, has its children at indexes 2 times 1 plus 1, which is 3, and 2 times 1 plus 2, which is 4: the values 7 and 4. Its parent is at index (1 minus 1) divided by 2, which is 0: the value 1.

blocks.text: So moving between a parent and its children is just arithmetic: **O(1)**, with no extra memory. Every heap operation in this course is built on these three formulas.

Put the two rules together. The shape rule holds automatically — an array has no gaps — so only the order rule needs checking: no parent may be bigger than either child. Only the first `⌊n / 2⌋` indexes have children, so the loop stops there.

blocks.caption: Each step compares one parent with its children. One smaller child is enough to fail.

blocks.code:
def is_min_heap(heap):
    n = len(heap)
    for i in range(n // 2):                        # only nodes that have a child
        left, right = 2 * i + 1, 2 * i + 2
        if heap[left] < heap[i]:                   # left child smaller than its parent
            return False
        if right < n and heap[right] < heap[i]:    # right child smaller
            return False
    return True                                    # no parent is bigger than a child

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1).** For a max-heap, flip both comparisons: no child may be **bigger** than its parent.

items: **build** a heap from n values at once: **O(n)** — faster than n pushes.
**find** any other value: **O(n)** — a heap only knows where its top is.

blocks.text: The next lesson shows how push and pop keep both rules intact in O(log n).

A **priority queue** is the idea: items come out in priority order instead of arrival order. A **heap** is how it's almost always built. That's why the libraries use both names: Python's module is `heapq`, Java's class is `PriorityQueue`, and C++'s is `priority_queue`.

items: A heap is a **complete binary tree** where every parent is ≤ its children (min-heap) or ≥ them (max-heap).
The **root** is the smallest (or largest) value: read it in **O(1)**.
Only the top is in order; the rest is **not sorted**.
It lives in an **array**: the children of `i` are at `2i + 1` and `2i + 2`, its parent at `⌊(i − 1) / 2⌋`.
